tasks.short: Judge where network adjustments are needed

steps.what: Monitor network performance on the view
Draft where future changes may be needed

loop.input: breach rows and the note template
loop.output: a note that cites system ids only
loop.check: Every cited system id is on the performance view
loop.stop: One pass, then drop any sentence with no system id
loop.why_not_simpler: Whether a future change is worth funding is not a fixed lookup

steps.what: Determine whether adjustments are needed
Apply the signed performance adjustments
File the future changes note

tasks.design: Network performance sits on a {BI} view with a system id and a threshold. A bounded note in {DOCS} drafts where future changes may be needed, citing only those rows. The systems administrator decides whether adjustments are needed now and applies them by hand. The future note is filed. Nothing changes unattended.
tasks.previous_blocker: Performance figures were copied into documents by hand, so a later reader could not see which hour a proposed change relied on.
tasks.enabler_now: Monitors can export a system id, a metric and a breach time that a note can cite.
tasks.still_hard: Whether an adjustment is worth the risk to live traffic is not a threshold.
tasks.human_edge: The administrator determines whether adjustments are needed and refuses a change the view does not support.

ambition.what: Review performance adjustments every month instead of only after a complaint

tasks.altitude: Less time assembling rows. The administrator can block an adjustment that cites no breach.

reach.task: Read where future changes are filed
reach.learn: Which adjustments were signed and which future changes are only noted

evidence.claim: Watching network performance is already a console habit. The slow part is copying figures into a case for a change.
Digest [S7] and [S8] describe a managed detection service that speeds investigation for mid-size firms, while a person still decides.
Digest [S13] reports an observational study of live security operations with shorter resolve times after a generative assistant versus matched peers. It was not a randomised trial.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so an unattended performance adjustment is out of scope.

assumptions: Focal role is the systems administrator. The task ends when they have decided whether adjustments are needed now and filed where future changes may be needed. A network redesign is out of scope.
Input contract: system id, metric, threshold, breach time, owner. Producer is the monitor export. A row with no system id is left off the note.
Native dashboards are configured before custom code. The modest meeting prior overstates this task: the time is on the view and the note. Applying an adjustment stays a person.
unknowns: Which metrics have no agreed threshold.
Who accepts a slower service if an adjustment waits.
Whether this firm is in scope of cyber duty of care rules.
research_questions: What share of breaches repeats the same system id?
How often is a proposed adjustment refused?

already_counted.description: Administrator edits the future changes draft
Hands-on adjustments stay with the administrator

incremental.description: Revise thresholds when a new system type is added

approvals.approved_version: adjustment decision signed for this review
the same signed adjustment decision and future note

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes exports lack a system id, so the note stays empty and the administrator still assembles the case. The high case assumes a clean note, while every adjustment is still done by hand. No unattended change is counted.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

steps.what: State computer hardware constraints
Design the computer hardware layout
Configure networking software in the lab
Test operating system software in the lab
Sign the tested operating software
Configure the signed software on the live system

tasks.design: The network architect states constraints on a {WORKFLOW} form. The systems administrator designs the computer hardware, configures networking software in a lab, and tests operating system software against a checklist in {DOCS}. Live configure runs only after they sign that test, and they do it themselves.
tasks.previous_blocker: Lab results lived in personal notes, so a live configure could not show which test it rested on.
tasks.enabler_now: A test checklist can store a software id, a hardware id and a pass or fail that the signature can cite.
tasks.still_hard: A new design is not a repeated job, and a failed test does not name the right next design.
tasks.human_edge: The administrator designs the change and refuses to configure software the test did not pass.
tasks.altitude: The checklist is shorter to file. Design, lab work and the live configure stay with the administrator.

reach.task: Read the signed test before asking for a live configure
reach.learn: Which software passed and which hardware is still in design

evidence.claim: Designing and testing hardware and software is still a person's work in a lab. The checklist is the part that can be a form. The design is not.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say that for firms in scope, the Dutch cyber duty of care includes patching. A test record can show what was tried. Scope depends on sector and size.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so an unattended configure of live software is out of scope.

assumptions: Focal role is the systems administrator. The task is design, configure and test of computer hardware, networking software and operating system software. Running the estate day to day is a different task.

Input contract: hardware id, software id, test id, pass or fail, constraint note. Producer of constraints is the network architect. Producer of results is the administrator. A test with no software id is not signed.
The meeting-heavy prior overstates workshops. Time is in the lab and at the console. Native install tools are used before custom code. Live configure is never unattended.
unknowns: Which software has no lab image.
Who signs when the administrator is absent.
Whether this firm is in scope of the cyber duty of care.
research_questions: What share of live configures has a filed test?
How often does the first lab test fail?

already_counted.description: Design time stays with the administrator
Live configure stays with the administrator

incremental.description: Extend the test checklist when a new software family appears

approvals.approved_version: test version signed for this software id

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes tests stay as free-text notes, so the checklist saves little and design is unchanged. The high case assumes the checklist is used, while design, lab configure and live configure all stay manual. No unattended live configure is counted.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Keep an inventory of emergency parts

steps.what: Count parts for emergency repairs
Maintain the inventory of parts
Mark inventory parts below the emergency line
State lead time for emergency repairs
Decide which emergency repairs parts to reorder

tasks.design: Counts of parts for emergency repairs go on a {WORKFLOW} form into a {SPREADSHEET}. Rows below the minimum are marked by rule. The vendor engineer states a lead time. The systems administrator decides what to reorder. Placing the purchase is a later task.
tasks.previous_blocker: The parts list was a private sheet with no minimum and no part id, so a shortfall was found only when a repair was already waiting.
tasks.enabler_now: A part id and a minimum can live in the same sheet the count updates.
tasks.still_hard: Someone still has to count what is on the shelf, and a wrong minimum orders the wrong parts.
tasks.human_edge: The administrator sets the minimum and decides which emergency repairs parts to reorder.

ambition.what: Review the parts minimum every quarter instead of only after a stock-out

tasks.altitude: Retyping the list shrinks. The count and the reorder decision stay with the administrator.

reach.task: Quote lead time for parts below the minimum
reach.learn: Which emergency parts are short and which minimums are current

evidence.claim: A parts inventory for emergency repairs is a count plus a list. The count is physical. The list is the part that gets retyped today.
The yearly meeting prior does not match this task. In a mid-size firm the work is a shelf count and a sheet, not a workshop.

assumptions: Focal role is the systems administrator. The task ends at a reorder decision. Buying the parts is the purchase task, not this one.
Input contract: part id, quantity on hand, minimum, site, repair use. Producer of the count is the administrator. A row with no part id is not marked short.
The sheet the firm already keeps is configured before a new store is built. The meeting-heavy prior is rejected: this is not a meeting.
unknowns: Who counts parts at a site the administrator does not visit.
Which parts have no stable id.
What minimum the business will fund.
research_questions: How many emergency parts sit below the minimum today?
How often is a repair delayed for a missing part?

already_counted.description: The shelf count stays with the administrator
The reorder decision stays with the administrator

incremental.description: Add a part id when a new spare type is stocked
Vendor time to refresh lead times after a price change

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes part ids are missing, so the shortfall rule rarely marks a row and the count stays fully manual. The high case assumes the list updates from the count, while every shelf count and every reorder decision still take administrator time. The purchase itself is not counted.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

steps.what: Read routine startup and shutdown procedures
Sign today's network startup procedures
Perform the signed network startup
Perform the signed network shutdown
Maintain control records for the run
Review control records when startup fails

tasks.design: Routine startup and shutdown procedures are a signed version in {DOCS}. The systems administrator still performs both on the {OPS_SYSTEM}. Control records for each run are written from the procedure id. A failed startup stays on a {BI} list for a person. The run is never unattended.
tasks.previous_blocker: Procedures were a printed sheet and control records were typed afterwards, so a failed start had no procedure version.
tasks.enabler_now: A procedure id can be stored with the run result, so the control record does not need a second typing.
tasks.still_hard: Starting or stopping a live network at the wrong time is costly, and some devices have no job interface.
tasks.human_edge: The administrator signs the procedures and performs the startup and the shutdown.
tasks.altitude: Control records file themselves. The administrator still performs startup and shutdown and can stop a run that looks wrong.

reach.task: Read control records after a failed startup
reach.learn: Which procedure version ran and which startup failed

evidence.claim: Routine network startup and shutdown in a mid-size firm is still a person at the console. The record of the run is the part that is retyped.
Digest [S22] says security logging must stay necessary and proportionate. A control record should store the procedure, the time and the result, not staff activity.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so an unattended startup or shutdown is out of scope.

assumptions: Focal role is the systems administrator. The task is routine startup and shutdown procedures and the control records of those runs.

Input contract: procedure id, system id, action (startup or shutdown), planned time, result. Producer of the procedure version is the administrator. A device with no procedure id is not on the signed list.

The meeting-heavy prior does not fit. Time is at the console. Native run records are configured before custom code. The signature is the procedure version for the period, not a new decision every morning. The morning act is still performed by hand.
unknowns: Which devices have no job interface.
Who may perform shutdown when the administrator is away.
Whether a night operator is allowed to start the network.
research_questions: How often does startup fail in a typical month?
What share of runs has no control record today?

already_counted.description: Procedure signature stays with the administrator
Hands-on startup stays with the administrator
Hands-on shutdown stays with the administrator

incremental.description: Revise procedure fields when a new device is added to the run

approvals.approved_version: startup and shutdown procedure version for this period

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes devices have no procedure id, so records stay manual and every run is unchanged. The high case assumes control records file from the procedure id, while startup and shutdown are still performed by hand. No unattended run is counted.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The administrator spends less time collecting performance rows and stock counts, and keeps startup, lab tests and adjustment choices.
reach: The network architect receives the filed note of future changes instead of a fresh export.
The vendor engineer sees which emergency parts are below the minimum before a call.
skills_to_grow: Separate a performance adjustment that is signed now from a future change that is only noted.
Treat a lab test of software as a checklist, and a live configure as a signed act.
Keep the parts inventory as fields a count can update, not a yearly rewrite.
role.ambitious_version: Performance notes, lab results, parts counts and control records are filed every time, and live startup still waits for the administrator.
